parts.note: Edward is the name of several English kings
Lear is the legendary king of Shakespeare's tragedy

explanation.surface: Royalty is introduced to a fellow from an Irish town.
explanation.walkthrough: One word, 'Kings', supplies two royal names in turn. 'Limerick' looks like the Irish city, but it is the five-line comic verse form the Victorian nonsense poet made famous.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian nonsense poet popularised the limerick verse form, so he is the archetypal limerick writer.

parts.note: the letter L written out in full as a word is spelt el or ell

explanation.surface: Someone pens a letter to a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter written' means a letter spelt out as a word rather than as a symbol: L written out is ELL. 'to' just joins it to A.
explanation.definitionFit: A common woman's given name, so it stands for a girl.

parts.note: the main is an old word for the open sea, and a disturbance on its surface is a moving ridge of water

explanation.surface: A piece of the principal commotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'main' reads as 'principal', but in crosswords it is often the sea, as in the Spanish Main.
explanation.definitionFit: A swell rising on the sea surface is a disturbance that forms part of the ocean.

clue.text: Rent vehicle to Pickwickian — a sleeper

parts.note: a rent is a tear, as is a rip
a van is a vehicle
Nathaniel Winkle is one of the members of the Pickwick Club in Dickens's Pickwick Papers

explanation.surface: Hiring a car to take a Dickens character who then falls asleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like hiring, but it is a noun: a tear.
explanation.definitionFit: Washington Irving's character slept for twenty years in the Catskill mountains, the classic fictional sleeper.

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for pound sterling, from Latin libra

indicators.note: changes says the letters of rate are rearranged

explanation.surface: The exchange rate for sterling shifts afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges RATE into ATER, put after L.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean afterwards, at a following time.

clue.text: Navy chaps put in a spot of decoration

indicators.note: put in says the navy men are placed inside the spot

parts.note: a dot is a spot
RN is the Royal Navy
chaps are men

explanation.surface: Sailors are placed in a spot of ornament on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: RN plus MEN goes inside A DOT, between D and the final OT.
explanation.definitionFit: An ornament or embellishment added to make something look better.

parts.note: E, east, is a point of the compass

indicators.note: turn says the word and is read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone points a finger and turns towards a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' reverses AND to DNA, after E.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, so a female person referred to as her.

clue.text: In time, poor Greene appears to grow worse

indicators.note: In says one piece is put inside the other

parts.note: a date is a point in time

indicators.note: poor says the letters of Greene are in bad shape and rearranged

explanation.surface: Graham Greene's writing is judged to decline over the years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' rearranges GREENE into EGENER, which goes inside DATE after the D.
explanation.definitionFit: To decline in quality or condition, to deteriorate.

clue.text: The silly fellow adopting one attitude calls for help

indicators.note: adopting says the fool takes on the next piece directly after him

parts.note: an ass is a foolish person
I is the Roman numeral for one
a stance is an attitude or position

explanation.surface: A fool striking a pose cries out to be rescued.
explanation.walkthrough: 'calls for' is only a link between the wordplay and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Aid or support given to someone is help.

parts.note: the heart here is the seat of the emotions, and the stimulant is a magic drink that arouses desire

explanation.surface: A drug that makes the heart beat faster.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase sounds like a cardiac drug, but the heart is the romantic one.
explanation.definitionFit: A philtre in folklore that makes the drinker fall in love, stirring the heart.

parts.note: in As You Like It, all the world's a stage and a man's acts are seven periods of life

explanation.surface: Performances by players in international affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: Jaques's speech in As You Like It says a man's 'acts being seven' stages of life, from infant to old age.
explanation.definitionFit: Jaques calls the stages of a lifetime the acts played on the world's stage.

clue.text: Perhaps assumed by Elizabethan women to be cheap drinks

parts.note: a farthing was the old British quarter-penny coin, so a farthing drink is a cheap one
ales are drinks of beer

explanation.surface: Tudor ladies were thought to like inexpensive beers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'assumed' means put on, as clothing, not supposed. A farthing was a quarter of an old British penny.
explanation.definitionFit: These hooped petticoats were worn under skirts by women in Elizabeth I's time.

clue.text: George is one of those little men — isn't as clumsy

parts.note: Pat is a short form of Patrick, a man's name cut down
Ron is a short form of Ronald, another man's name cut down

indicators.note: clumsy says the letters of isn't as are put together awkwardly in a new order

explanation.surface: George is mocked as one of the small men who are awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little men' gives two shortened male names. 'clumsy' rearranges ISNTAS into SAINTS. St George is England's patron saint.
explanation.definitionFit: St George is the protector saint of England, one of the saints adopted as guardians of a country or trade.

clue.text: Man gets one out of a tree

indicators.note: out of says the letters of gets one are knocked out of shape and rearranged

explanation.surface: A man takes one fruit down from a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' rearranges GETSONE into GOSTEEN, after MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A tropical Asian tree bearing a sweet purple fruit.

indicators.note: into says the shuffled word goes inside the friends

parts.note: allies are friends

indicators.note: breaking says the letters of Ergo are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Therefore, interrupting the stories one's companions tell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' rearranges ERGO into EGOR, which goes 'into' ALLIES after ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: Stories with a hidden moral or symbolic meaning are a kind of tale.

parts.note: letting suggests renting out property for cash, but it also means permitting, and the word for a sum given regularly also means permission

explanation.surface: Rental income from a property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letting' looks like renting out a house; read as 'permitting' it names the act of permitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Pocket money given regularly is so called, and the same word means the act of permitting.

clue.text: Little boy takes relatives a measure of liquor

parts.note: a nipper is a small child, a little boy
kin are relatives

explanation.surface: A youngster brings his family a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes' is only a link between the two pieces and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a small measure of drink, about half a pint or less.

clue.text: Perhaps the best known pottery centre

definitions.text: Perhaps the best known pottery centre

parts.words: Perhaps the best known pottery centre
parts.note: the middle of the word pottery is otter, so this is the most famous otter in fiction

explanation.surface: Possibly the most famous place where ceramics are made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pottery centre' reads as a place like Stoke, but the middle letters of 'pottery' spell OTTER. Henry Williamson's novel Tarka the Otter made this one famous.
explanation.definitionFit: The otter hero of Henry Williamson's 1927 novel, the best-known otter in English literature.

definitions.meaning: fresh as in new or unripe
a golf putting surface, which has the hole in it

explanation.surface: Something new with a hole in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Inexperienced or unripe fruit is called fresh in this sense, and on a golf course the putting surface holds the cup.

clue.text: Like the country-lover taking port in quiet room

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet

indicators.note: taking says the quiet room takes the port in, holding it inside

parts.note: an attic is a room under the roof
Rio de Janeiro is a Brazilian port

explanation.surface: A nature-lover drinks port in a peaceful room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'country-lover' suggests someone who loves the countryside, but it is someone who loves their nation. RIO goes inside PATTIC after PAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Devoted to one's nation, as a lover of their homeland is.

clue.text: On the short side — is he Lord Hugh, possibly ?

indicators.note: possibly says the letters of is he Lord Hugh may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Asking whether a nobleman called Lord Hugh is rather small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges all the letters of IS HE LORD HUGH. A short person may reach only as high as a taller one's shoulder.
explanation.definitionFit: Reaching up only to a taller person's upper arm, which describes someone of small stature beside them.

clue.text: Female goes to church in future

parts.note: a hen is a female bird
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A woman will attend church from now on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes to' just joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An old sense meaning from this time on, henceforth.

indicators.note: upsets herself says the girl's name turned upside down or backwards stays the same

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A young woman gets herself into a state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsets' looks like distressing, but it means turning over: the name reads the same backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A common woman's given name, so it stands for a girl.

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the run of words workhouse daily

explanation.surface: A pauper set to work every day in the poorhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the join of 'workhouse daily'. A workhouse was the Victorian institution where the poor were housed and set to work.
explanation.definitionFit: Put to service or occupied, as a tool or worker is.

indicators.note: retreat says one letter of the country falls back to a later place in the word

parts.note: Eire is the Irish name for Ireland

explanation.surface: A lake set in a rural hideaway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the country' is Eire; 'retreat' makes its I fall back two places, giving the lake.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the five Great Lakes of North America.

clue.text: Peel has, hard things to do for niggardly people

parts.note: the peel of a fruit is its skin
flints are very hard stones

explanation.surface: Peel holds tough tasks for mean people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' and 'to do for' just link the pieces and the definition; Peel looks like the Victorian prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Misers who hate to spend money, mean or stingy folk.

parts.note: a mouth organ is a harmonica, but here it is an organ of the face, and the one above the mouth is the smelling organ

explanation.surface: Pitched above the notes of a harmonica.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mouth organ' looks like a harmonica and 'Higher' like pitch, but the organ sits on the face above the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The smelling organ sits on the face just above the mouth.

parts.note: under means less than, as in under ten
to stand something is to bear it

explanation.surface: Notice fewer than a bear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bear' looks like the animal, but it is the verb meaning tolerate.
explanation.definitionFit: To see a point is to grasp or comprehend it.
